evaluation.positioning_hook: A CIA trainee with a history of coercive abuse discovers her agency’s neural warfare program is rewriting reality, forcing her to choose between the man she loves and the system that built her.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has immediate commercial lift: CIA training, mind-control tech, and a rooftop assassination clock give it a clean thriller promise with a strong female lead. The audience is clear and the hook is easy to sell, though the dense lore and psychological layering narrow it a bit from four-quadrant simplicity.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early and keeps sharpening: ARC turns training into lived reality, then the script reveals the lived reality may itself be manufactured. The opening Istanbul op, the Georgetown lecture, and the Farm all point to the same engine with escalating clarity.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ridley is a strong engine: smart, wounded, skeptical, and operationally gifted, with a contradiction between empathy and tactical ruthlessness. Ian, Egan, Alvarez, and Dawson all have distinct functions, though Ridley is clearly the center of gravity.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The ARC system is a fresh sci-fi device, and the script uses it in a way that is both tactical and psychological rather than just decorative. The repeated reality-overwrite structure and the final cycle reveal give it a confident, high-concept swing.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script is built on escalating tests, reversals, and reveals, and it keeps moving from training to live op with very little dead air. The final act especially tightens the screws with the Markov/Kerrigan decoy, rooftop confrontation, and cycle reveal.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea feels both novel and legible: a predictive-intelligence program that weaponizes trauma and perception. It has the kind of instantly graspable weirdness that can travel, even if the mythology gets elaborate by the end.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The CIA Farm, ARC backlot, neural patches, card system, and live-op mirroring create a world with rules and hierarchy, not just a backdrop. The intelligence ecosystem feels operationally specific, and the simulated locations generate story rather than merely hosting it.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a distinct register: sleek intelligence-thriller mechanics fused with psychological horror and romantic memory fracture. The tonal identity is consistent enough to feel ownable, especially in the way the HUD language and emotional flashbacks collide.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The script keeps revealing that the obvious story is only the surface: ARC, the cycles, the implanted memories, and Ridley’s relationship to Ian all point to deeper machinery. The final reveal that her life has been iterated gives the premise unusually strong rewatch and interpretation value.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Ridley/Ian is the main relational engine, but the script also gives real friction to Alvarez, Egan, Harrison, Dawson, and West. The ensemble is functional and story-generating, though it still lives or dies on the central Ridley/Ian dynamic.

lead_characters.name: Ridley Cooper
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, 20s, CIA trainee / cognitive psychology background, survivor of coercive abuse and school violence.
lead_characters.hook: Ridley is the script’s moral and emotional center: brilliant, guarded, and instinctively suspicious of systems that claim to know better than people. She’s a trauma expert who can read coercion in others, but her own reality has been engineered so thoroughly that every instinct becomes both weapon and liability.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is showcase territory in the vein of Jodie Comer in Killing Eve or Elisabeth Moss in The Handmaid’s Tale: a role that demands intelligence, fragility, steel, and escalating paranoia in the same performance. It gives an actor the rare chance to play tactical competence, romantic ache, and identity collapse while carrying a franchise-level concept.

lead_characters.name: Ian Walsh
lead_characters.demographics: Man, mid-20s to early 30s, CIA operative / trainee, physically capable, emotionally disciplined.
lead_characters.hook: Ian is the idealized operator who slowly reveals the cost of being optimized: he’s charming, lethal, and deeply trained to trust the system over his own conscience. His bond with Ridley gives the script its emotional voltage, and his eventual fracture is the story’s most painful proof that ARC can rewrite a person from the inside out.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Adam Driver in Marriage Story or Michael B. Jordan in Creed II room to be controlled on the surface and volatile underneath. It offers a strong actor a physical-action showcase with a buried-romantic core and a late-breaking emotional reversal.

lead_characters.name: Dawson
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 40s, intelligence/defense technologist with ambiguous agency ties.
lead_characters.hook: Dawson is the script’s most unnerving institutional face: polished, calm, and always one layer removed from accountability. He sells ARC as progress while functioning like the system’s human interface, and the West/Dawson identity bleed makes him feel like a predator hiding inside bureaucracy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do the controlled menace of Michael Emerson in Person of Interest or Giancarlo Esposito in Breaking Bad. The appeal is in playing authority as seduction, then letting the mask slip just enough to terrify.

lead_characters.name: Alvarez
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, 20s, data analytics trainee, smart, guarded, observant.
lead_characters.hook: Alvarez is the clearest counterweight to ARC’s certainty: she understands systems, but she’s not seduced by them. She becomes the story’s quiet truth-teller, the one who can translate data into moral ambiguity without losing her nerve.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong supporting territory in the mode of Auli’i Cravalho in The Power or Jurnee Smollett in Lovecraft Country: sharp, emotionally legible, and smarter than the room. It gives an actor a grounded intelligence role with real authority in ensemble scenes.

lead_characters.name: Egan
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 20s, West Point legacy, tactical trainee, physically aggressive, status-driven.
lead_characters.hook: Egan is the dangerous believer: competitive, cocky, and eager to let the machine validate his worst instincts. He’s not just a rival; he’s the script’s clearest example of how ARC rewards aggression and punishes hesitation until the moral cost becomes visible.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the swagger-and-crack energy of Jesse Plemons in Game Night or Taylor Kitsch in Friday Night Lights. The showcase is a slow turn from alpha confidence into moral panic.

lead_characters.name: Wyatt Denny
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 20s, worst-case-scenarios analyst, socially awkward, hyper-alert.
lead_characters.hook: Denny is the anxious observer in a room full of operators, the one who sees the cost before the others do. He’s a useful pressure valve in the ensemble and a reminder that the system’s logic can be understood without being trusted.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play nervous intelligence with bite, like Paul Dano in Escape at Dannemora or Ben Schwartz in serious-mode ensemble work. It’s a character-part that can steal scenes by being the first to notice the truth.

lead_characters.name: Chris Williams
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 20s, cybersecurity trainee, quiet, focused, vulnerable to overload.
lead_characters.hook: Williams is the script’s most tragic cautionary figure: the guy who follows the prompts until the prompts don’t stop. His breakdown gives the story its clearest human cost for sensory manipulation, and he becomes the proof that ARC can outlive the mission inside the operator’s head.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the breakdown territory of Rami Malek in Mr. Robot or Lakeith Stanfield in Sorry to Bother You. The showcase is the collapse from competence into terror, with a real emotional aftershock.

lead_characters.name: Sykes
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 50s-60s, seasoned operations director, institutional hardliner.
lead_characters.hook: Sykes is the old-guard pragmatist who treats human beings as mission variables and calls it discipline. He’s not flashy, but he gives the script its institutional spine and its coldest articulation of the program’s ethics.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong authority-role territory in the vein of J.K. Simmons in Whiplash or Bryan Cranston in a command role: controlled, intimidating, and all business. The appeal is in playing a man who believes moral discomfort is a luxury.

lead_characters.name: Bill Harrison
lead_characters.demographics: Man, older, lead ops trainer, smart, deadly, institutional veteran.
lead_characters.hook: Harrison is the trainer who knows exactly how the machine works and has no interest in pretending otherwise. He’s a clean, efficient embodiment of the Farm’s doctrine, and his calm makes the program feel even more normalized.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the dry command presence of David Strathairn or Lance Reddick. It’s a precision-support part with authority, menace, and institutional weight.

lead_characters.name: Cameron West
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 50s, professor / abuser / projected identity construct.
lead_characters.hook: West is the story’s emotional ghost and its most personal villain: the abusive figure whose face keeps reappearing inside ARC’s manipulations. Whether he’s literal, simulated, or weaponized memory, he functions as the embodiment of control that Ridley has to outgrow.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do the chilling intimacy of Michael Shannon in Take Shelter or Ben Mendelsohn in Bloodline. The showcase is menace without volume, with the added twist of identity instability.

lead_characters.name: Senator Kerrigan
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 50s, U.S. senator, military family background, public-facing reformer.
lead_characters.hook: Kerrigan is the political pressure point: a public skeptic of ARC who still gets pulled into its orbit. He gives the script a credible civic counterweight and a late-game moral ambiguity that keeps the ending from feeling purely procedural.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the gravitas of Jeff Daniels in The Newsroom or Mark Ruffalo in Spotlight. The appeal is in playing public conscience with just enough private vulnerability to complicate the politics.

casting_characteristics: Lead requires a performer who can carry action, psychological fracture, and romantic memory
Several roles are age-specific but not highly restrictive

notable_requirements: Multiple international city looks created through backlot overwrite and selective real-world exteriors
Rooftop embassy-row climax in Washington, D.C.
Server room / observation deck / training bay / tactical house builds

technical.vfx_details: Extensive HUD overlays, reality-overwrite transitions, digital face-shift moments, simulated city transformations, and final-cycle memory reconstructions.
technical.sfx_needs: Gunfire, explosions, practical fight choreography, vehicle movement, rooftop falls, and simulated mission destruction.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: streamer original or theatrical-to-streaming action-thriller with premium genre positioning

budget.note: Contemporary setting keeps the base spend contained, but the repeated city overwrites, HUD-heavy visual language, rooftop action, and multiple international looks will push this above a simple contained-thriller build.

casting.note: Ridley is the load-bearing role and needs a performer who can sell intelligence, trauma, action, and romantic memory; Ian and Dawson also need actors with strong control and menace. The ensemble is manageable, but the lead is not generic.

development.note: The final-cycle reveal, the West/Dawson identity bleed, and the question of what is real versus implanted are the script’s main development pressure points. Buyers will want clarity on how much of the mythology is literal versus psychological before committing.

comp_set.title: Source Code
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the high-concept mission loop and the tension between operational precision and emotional truth.

comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the predictive-policing premise and the anxiety of a system that claims to know the future.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like smart, high-concept action thrillers with a strong female lead and a romantic/psychological edge.
audience_target.demographics: 18-49 skew, slightly male-leaning for the action hook but with strong female appeal through Ridley’s POV and emotional stakes.

budget_tier.note: Modern-day spy action, moderate VFX, multiple city looks, and a rooftop climax keep this in the mid-budget feature lane.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of smart, commercial genre with a prestige sheen: a concept-forward thriller that still wants action set pieces and a strong emotional spine. It is especially attractive to buyers looking for a female-led franchise starter without tentpole spend.

ip_potential.detail: The ARC world can support a sequel or spin-off centered on a different operative cycle or a different intelligence cell using the same neural system; the West/Dawson machinery also opens a prequel angle around the program’s origin.

strengths.what_it_means: That makes the project easy to pitch, easy to market, and easy for a buyer to understand in one pass. It gives the script a clean commercial identity in a crowded genre lane.
strengths.evidence: The ARC system turns training into lived reality, then reveals the lived reality may itself be a constructed cycle.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Ridley is a real lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: A role with this much intelligence, trauma, and tactical competence can attract serious actors and elevate the package fast. It also gives the movie a durable emotional center beyond the tech conceit.
strengths.evidence: Her lecture on coercive control, her refusal to trust prompts, and her final decision to override ARC define her arc.

strengths.what_it_means: Each reveal naturally raises the stakes from training exercise to live op to identity crisis, which is exactly what a producer wants in a commercial thriller. That structure supports strong trailers and a clear act-to-act sales pitch.
strengths.evidence: Istanbul, Georgetown, the Farm, the live D.C. op, and the cycle reveal all escalate the same premise.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The world feels operational, not decorative.
strengths.what_it_means: That makes the script feel expensive in the right way: specific, procedural, and story-generating rather than generic spy wallpaper. Buyers like worlds that create scenes, not just settings.
strengths.evidence: The card system, neural patch, observation decks, live-op mirroring, and training metrics all drive plot choices.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The emotional engine is not just tech.
strengths.what_it_means: The romance and abuse-memory material gives the movie a second lane beyond concept, which broadens audience attachment and actor interest. It also keeps the story from feeling like a pure gadget thriller.
strengths.evidence: Ridley and Ian’s repeated memory flashes, the West intrusion, and the final recognition scene give the thriller a human wound.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, high-concept sci-fi thriller with a strong female lead, a marketable intelligence-world hook, and enough action to play as a real event package. The script’s biggest commercial advantage is that the concept, the emotional wound, and the production footprint all point in the same direction: a mid-budget, streamer-friendly genre buy that can be sold fast and cast up.

items.area: The final-cycle reveal is a lot of machinery.
items.detail: The script’s last-act architecture stacks implanted memories, repeated cycles, identity bleed, and a West/Dawson morph into one reveal package. That gives the movie a strong twist, but it also creates a buyer conversation about how much mythology the audience needs to track in the final 20 minutes.

items.area: Ridley carries most of the dramatic weight.
items.detail: The script gives her the clearest arc, the strongest emotional wound, and the most decisive choices, while the rest of the ensemble functions more as pressure systems than fully independent engines. That is fine for a feature, but it means the package rises or falls on the lead attachment conversation.

items.area: The HUD language can get dense.
items.detail: The card prompts, confidence scores, overlays, and mission-status readouts are part of the movie’s identity, but they also create a lot of on-screen information to process. In a buyer room, that reads as a clarity note: the concept is strong, but the execution will need disciplined visual grammar.

items.area: The action is smart, not cheap.
items.detail: The rooftop chase, live D.C. operation, city overwrites, and repeated international environments keep this out of micro-budget territory. It is still manageable, but the script is asking for enough visual and stunt support that the production plan matters from day one.

issues.headline: The main friction is not the premise; it’s the amount of mythology the ending asks the audience to absorb while the movie is still moving at thriller speed. The other buyer-level concern is practical: this is a mid-budget package, not a contained indie, so the concept has to justify the spend with clean execution and a strong lead attachment.
